assessment:
In this study, Strobl and Gamazon introduce a novel framework for identifying root causal genes—gene expression levels directly regulated by unobserved root causes (genetic and environmental factors) that have large causal effects on disease phenotypes. The authors distinguish root causal genes from previously defined concepts such as core genes (which directly cause disease) and driver genes (which account for somatic mutations in cancer), positioning their work as addressing the earliest changes in gene expression that initiate disease pathogenesis. They develop the Root Causal Strength (RCS) metric to quantify the magnitude of conditional causal effects of unobserved error terms without requiring direct estimation of these terms or imposing restrictive distributional assumptions. The Root Causal Strength using Perturbations (RCSP) algorithm integrates high-throughput Perturb-seq data to learn causal structure and bulk RNA-seq data to compute patient-specific RCS scores.

The methodological innovation is substantial. The authors provide rigorous theoretical foundations, including an asymptotic argument that eliminates the need for sequencing depth normalization by leveraging the Poisson approximation of measurement error when library sizes are large (≥10 million reads in bulk RNA-seq). They prove Fisher consistency of RCSP under unconditional d-separation faithfulness, a weaker assumption than typically required. The algorithm transfers only binary causal relations (not functional forms) from single-cell Perturb-seq to bulk RNA-seq, enhancing robustness to cross-platform differences. In synthetic experiments with 2,500 genes across 30 replicates, RCSP substantially outperformed state-of-the-art methods (ANM, LiNGAM, CausalCell) and standard regression approaches, with all pairwise comparisons significant after Bonferroni correction. The method maintained low error across different cluster numbers and remained robust to cyclic graphs and discrepancies between Perturb-seq and bulk RNA-seq causal structures.

Applications to age-related macular degeneration (AMD, 513 samples, 2,077 genes) and multiple sclerosis (MS, 137 samples, 6,882 genes) demonstrate biological validity. RCSP correctly identified age as the dominant root cause in AMD (D-RCS = 0.46, more than double the nearest gene). The algorithm detected few root causal genes but many correlated genes in both diseases, supporting an "omnigenic root causal model" where sparse upstream root causes affect many downstream genes. Top-ranked genes in AMD (MIPEP, SLC7A5, HEATR1) and MS (MNT, CERCAM, HERPUD2) map onto known pathogenic pathways involving oxidative stress and T cell infiltration, respectively, with pathway enrichment analyses identifying biologically relevant mechanisms (amino acid transport in AMD; APC-AXIN and EPH-ephrin signaling in MS) at FDR < 5%. Drug enrichment analyses identified therapeutically relevant compounds, including cathepsin inhibitors for an MS patient subgroup. Hierarchical clustering revealed patient subgroups with distinct root causal profiles, including correct identification of EPH-ephrin enrichment in relapsing-remitting MS patients.

The study has notable limitations that the authors transparently acknowledge. The claim that "no existing algorithms attempt to identify root causal genes" is difficult to verify without comprehensive literature review, though the conceptual distinction from existing methods is clear. RCS quantifies conditional causal strength rather than unconditional causal effect, though empirical results suggest these align well in practice (~95% agreement in direction). The method achieves patient-specificity but not cell-type specificity due to reliance on bulk RNA-seq phenotypic labels. RCSP can only analyze genes present in Perturb-seq datasets (currently thousands rather than all genes) and cannot adjust for unknown confounding. The directed acyclic graph assumption may not hold for time-varying biological processes. Despite these limitations, the work represents a significant methodological advance with clear therapeutic implications, providing a principled, scalable, and disease-agnostic approach to identifying upstream targets for disease intervention.
